# Representative government (elected assembly) (`representative_government`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by rule_of_law, secret_ballot, peaceful_transfer_of_power, public_accounts_audit
- Core idea: Eligible voters choose delegates for a term. The electorate has ranged from a few property holders to nearly all adult citizens. A representative assembly must consent to taxes and laws, can question ministers, and can be voted out. It solves two problems: a state too large for everyone to meet, and a ruler who needs money but cannot be trusted. The ruler gains too, because taxes that have been consented to are paid with less resistance and lenders trust a debt the assembly has voted. Minimum design: regular sessions the ruler cannot skip, control of the purse, free speech inside the chamber, and re-election so members stay answerable.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating elections as the essence: historically consent to taxation and the right to refuse came first, and the vote was limited to property holders for centuries
  - Elections without a secret ballot, a voter roll and a loser who accepts the result produce bought votes and civil war
  - Calling Athens a representative democracy: Athenians voted in person and filled most offices by lot; they regarded election as aristocratic
  - Assuming assemblies were a European invention: Indian republics, the Old Assyrian city assembly, Carthage and many African and American polities governed by councils
  - An assembly the ruler summons only when he likes (French Estates General, not called 1614–1789) is no check at all
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1900 BC – the city assembly of Assur and its annually chosen eponym official share power with the ruler (Kanesh letters); Jacobsen's wider 'primitive democracy' thesis is disputed; india: c. 6th–4th c. BC – gana-sangha republics such as the Vajji/Licchavi governed by assemblies of clan heads; c. 920 Uttaramerur inscriptions set rules for Chola village committees; greece: 508/507 BC – Cleisthenes' reforms at Athens: assembly of all citizens and a council of 500; direct, not representative; rome: 509 BC (traditional) – Republic with popular assemblies electing magistrates, voting by groups weighted towards the rich; africa: Carthage (by 4th c. BC) elected suffetes with senate and assembly, praised by Aristotle; councils and age-set assemblies among Igbo, Oromo and others in later centuries; islamic: 7th c. – consultation (shura) is a principle but no elected body follows; the 1876 constitution provides for a parliament, which first meets in 1877; europe: 930 – Icelandic Althing; 1188 Cortes of León with elected townsmen; 1265 Montfort's parliament and 1295 Model Parliament in England; 1689 Parliament supreme over taxation; americas: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Grand Council of clan-appointed chiefs, founded between the 12th and 16th c. (date disputed); 1619 Virginia House of Burgesses; 1789 US Congress; china: 1909 – first elected provincial assemblies
- Read:
  - Bernard Manin, The Principles of Representative Government (1997)
  - David Stasavage, The Decline and Rise of Democracy (2020)
  - John Stuart Mill, Considerations on Representative Government (1861)
